Tried it and cleared an inbox they had been putting off for weeks in about 10 minutes. They like that it's tied to Gmail because they can move back anytime by deleting the Shortwave account, so it feels low risk. It also imported all their aliases and signatures.

A Front user said Shortwave's grouping/'Bundles' is 'top shelf', especially the interface and speed. They called it a better organizational layer than tags, folders or merging emails, and found manually bundling by drag-and-drop 'superb'. They also praised the design as gorgeous and thoughtful compared with Front's tags/folders mess.

The same Front user said it would be really hard to leave Front, citing Front's private team comments for collaborating on responses. They didn't care for Shortwave's Workspaces/chat or the gif/emoji features, since they see email as formal communication.

While trying it, a user liked the grouping and 'mark as done' features. But the print and UI elements were tiny, so they had to zoom in a lot, and it was hard to see at a glance who emails are from. They felt the design favors being pretty over being functional and that the typography needs attention.

A Google Inbox refugee was interested, but said $9/mo for an email client doesn't make sense for a personal user. They worried the free plan's 90-day limit would be annoying enough not to risk linking their Gmail account.

On pricing: they have spent $0 on email clients in 20 years, and at $9/mo Shortwave would add up to thousands. For turning Gmail back into Google Inbox they'd consider a one-time $20 fair, maybe stretching to $60.

On the free plan, emails older than 90 days don't appear in search and pre-signup history beyond 90 days isn't imported. One user called this a showstopper: when searching you need to know whether you got something, and this would cut them off from old email.
'No thank you.. all these apps either want way too many gmail permissions, and/or are hosted.' The user would rather stick with IMAP and is trying to get off Gmail anyway.

After reading the privacy policy, a user said 'hard pass'. The policy covers collecting email contents and metadata and sharing personal data with vendors such as hosting, CRM and analytics providers. They would prefer a local client, especially for business email.

A user was uncomfortable that everything syncs to Shortwave's servers even with the desktop app, given sensitive emails like OTPs, account resets and bank authorizations. They wished for a denylist so certain mail is never synced.

A security consultant who relies on PGP said they can't use a web mail client for security reasons. With Shortwave only working with Google, it likely won't ever be for them; they'd rather pay for Thunderbird with some of these features.

Several users asked for IMAP support and lamented that it only works with Gmail. One FastMail user said they would gladly pay a yearly subscription for a good cross-platform client but is anti-Google, so Shortwave is out.

A user felt the product 'has been done before and doesn't seem to solve much or save much time', saying Hey.com seems better for personal email problems. They added that it wants to be a business tool without core features like Front's multi-inbox, and found the demo video voiceover 'awful'.

A user's ongoing challenge with all these email apps: Gmail is the foundation they build on with other tools. Especially on mobile, they want to know how Shortwave integrates with common extensions like HubSpot.
A user asked why there is no delete button in Shortwave.

One user said a product promising a 'more enjoyable' inbox that advertises with cat pictures and lunch threads misses the mark. They don't want more fluff or faster emailing, and would rather have tools that reduce email.

A GTD practitioner said they'd never pay for it. Automatically organizing email organizes noise, which would mean more work for them in the long run. They want tools that extract information out of email into one central system instead.
A user noted that the layout and color palette are 'strongly evocative of Inbox', so they presumed it was trying to recreate Google Inbox.
